blocks.p: Relay room, Serenity, the lower workings. Service ticket on a household Pearl, closed.

ARDEN, Joss, drill crew, north shafts. Complaint: his mother, ascended from the old south dome, says the same thing at every visit, in the same words. Checked: relay clean, signal clean, the ascended present and content. Repetition within tolerance. Householder advised that the ascended are very happy. Closed, O. Fell. The householder has opened this ticket eleven times before.
Joss Arden had been under the ice when it came down, and he was taking all afternoon to die.

The infirmary of the lower workings was nothing like the Mercy Office’s holding house. It was a long, low chamber with a sagging ceiling of insulated panels, crowded with cots and cabinets and the smell of antiseptic, and the lights were the hard white of a place where people needed to see what they were doing. Most of the cots were empty. The one at the far end had a curtain drawn half around it, and inside the curtain a big man lay on his back with his chest bound in a pressure wrap and a mask over his mouth, and every breath he took made a sound like something being dragged.

“Crush injuries to the chest and pelvis,” the medic said. She was a short, square woman named Tamsin Oyel with her sleeves rolled to the elbow, and she spoke to Sol without looking away from the monitor. “Ribs, lungs, liver. He’s bleeding inside faster than I can put it back. On Concord they might have saved him. Here I can keep him comfortable.” She glanced at him then. “I’m sorry, Your Grace. We don’t have much to work with this far out.”
“I know.”
“The backup’s clean. I checked it twice.” She lowered her voice. “Father Crane asked for you specially.”

The chaplain was waiting just outside the curtain, a narrow young-faced priest named Wendel Crane with his hands knotted together in front of his robe. He bowed so low that Sol had to touch his shoulder to bring him up.

“Thank you for coming, Your Grace. I didn’t know what else to do.” He spoke quickly and quietly. “Two of the five on Serenity were mine. I did everything right. I said every word. And they came back.” He swallowed. “One of them was Hanne Lusk. Last autumn she was near the front of the Renewal queue at the chapel door, and a man came in late off the shafts, a stranger, and she gave him her place. Stepped out of the line and went and stood at the back.” He shook his head as though it still astonished him. “I’d never heard of such a thing. Nobody had. The Renewal office wrote to ask me whether she was well.” He looked down at his knotted hands. “I’d rather not lose a third.”
Lose. It was not a church word. Sol let it go by.
“Tell me about him.”
“Joss Arden. A hundred and forty-two. Drill crew, north shafts, eighty years. Married. No children.” Crane hesitated. “A good man. Very regular at the Pearl. He visits his mother every week.”
Sol went in behind the curtain.

The miner’s wife was sitting on a stool by the cot with her husband’s big hand in both of hers. She was a lean, fair woman with her hair tied back and the grey coverall of the processing plant still on, and she looked up at Sol with polite, open interest, as if he were a visitor she had been expecting at a slightly inconvenient time.
“Your Grace. I’m Rena. Thank you for coming down.”
“I’m sorry it’s for this.”
“Oh, well.” She looked at her husband. “It happens. They’ve been saying for years that the north shafts weren’t sound.” She patted his hand. “Joss. The bishop’s here.”
The man’s eyes opened. They were pale blue and very clear, the only part of him that did not seem to be hurting. They went to Sol’s robes and then to his face.
“Your Grace,” he said, behind the mask. His voice was almost nothing.
“Don’t try to talk.”
“Want to.” The eyes held on him. “Is it far?”
Sol pulled the second stool close and sat. “No farther than the Pearl.”
“My mother’s there.” Each word cost him a breath. “Went up when I was a boy. Breach in the old south dome. I was at school.” He closed his eyes and opened them. “I go every week. To see her.”
“Then she’ll be waiting for you.”
“Always says the same thing.” Something moved at the corner of his mouth that might have been a smile. “Every week. Same thing.”
His wife squeezed his hand fondly. “She’s very happy there.”
“That’s what she says,” Joss said.

He did not say anything after that. Sol sat with him through the rest of the afternoon, and Rena sat on the other side, and Pell stood quietly against the far wall with his tablet held against his chest, and the medic came and went. Rena talked a little, in a pleasant, easy voice, about the plant and the shift roster and whether the crew’s pay for the month would still come to her.

“He sent half of it away, you know,” she told Sol, the way a woman mentions her husband’s taste for some odd food. “Every month, for years. To people on the far workings he’d never met. I never understood it. We had plenty.” She smoothed the blanket over the big hand. “I suppose it’ll all come to me now.”

Once she laughed at something she had said herself. Joss’s breathing grew slower and further apart, and began to come in long hoarse pulls with silences between them, each silence longer than the last, and in each silence Sol found that he was waiting, without meaning to, for the next breath to come.
The last one came a little before the shift bell. It was a deep, rough breath, almost a gasp, and then there was a silence, and the silence went on.
The monitor gave a single soft tone. The medic leaned in, looked, and touched it quiet. She glanced at the clock on the wall and said the time aloud, to no one in particular.
Rena let go of the hand and laid it neatly on the blanket. “There,” she said. “That’s done.”

Sol stood. He laid two fingers on the dead man’s temple, where the Halo lay under skin that was still warm, and closed his eyes, and the rite opened in the corner of his sight in its gold script. Joss Arden, kept through the fire, renewed in the new creation, received into Life.
“You were kept through the fire,” he said. “You were renewed in the new creation. Now go up into Life, and see the City of the Throne.”
He signed it.

He held his breath through the moment, as he always did. On the wall above the cot, a small terminal showed what the ascension clerk would have shown him in the cathedral: a line of gold light climbing steadily from left to right as the backup went up. It reached the end of the line.
It stopped there.
Then, very gently, in the same gold script, the terminal said: Not received.
Behind him Sol heard Crane draw a breath that was almost a sound.
“Again,” Sol said.

The chaplain resubmitted. The gold line climbed. It reached the end. Not received. Again. Not received. The fourth time, a second line of text came up beneath the first, smaller, in the plain grey script of a system message rather than a rite. The vessel could not be resolved.
“Is something wrong?” Rena asked.
“A delay,” Crane said. His voice shook. “A technical delay. We’ll keep trying.”
“Oh, good.” She stood and smoothed the front of her coverall. “Will that be tonight, or should I come back tomorrow?”
Then her face changed.

It happened so quickly that Sol was not sure afterward he had seen it. Her mouth pulled down at one corner and her chin drew up and creased, and her eyes went wide and wet and fixed on the big still hand she had laid on the blanket, and for an instant she looked like no one Sol had ever seen, like a picture from the archives of the old world. Her hand went up to her temple.
And then her face smoothed, as if a hand had passed over it.
“I’m sorry, Your Grace,” she said, puzzled, a little embarrassed. “I don’t know what that was.”
“It’s quite all right,” Sol said.

She went out. Sol stayed where he was. The medic had begun to unfasten the pressure wrap, quietly and competently, and she drew the sheet up over the miner’s face, and then there was only the long shape of him under the cloth and the big hand still showing at the edge. There would be no Pearl brightening for him, no figure gathering in the light. The backup would sit in its holding place in the relay for a few weeks and lose coherence, as Vasque had said, and then there would be nothing. Joss Arden was simply dead, the way people had been dead in the old world before the mercy. Sol could not remember the last time he had stood beside someone who was simply dead.

There was something in his throat. It was a tightness, low down, like a hand closing, and it did not go away when he swallowed. He did not have a name for it. He stood beside the cot until Pell touched his sleeve.

The relay room was two levels down, a cramped chamber of humming racks and cold air, and the two technicians on shift stood up when the bishop came in. The senior one, a stout grey-voiced man named Orrin Fell, had the relay logs open before Sol had finished asking for them.

“Transient fault, Your Grace. Almost certainly. These relays went in two hundred years ago, and the ice plays havoc with the lines. We’ve had Concord out twice.” He spread the logs in the air between them: the gold climb of the backup, the flat stop at the top. “Clean going up. Clean all the way to the gate. Then it bounces. Hardware, I’d put money on it.”
“But the other ascensions from Serenity go through.”
“Most of them, Your Grace. That’s what makes it transient.” Fell smiled. He had a pleasant, unworried face. “I’ll file the report for the administrator. Excuse me a moment. I’ll get you a copy.”

He stepped out into the corridor. The junior technician, a thin, dark-eyed young woman whose tag read Quill, had not sat down again. She was looking at Sol with the expression of someone standing at the edge of cold water.
“It isn’t the hardware,” she said.
Pell made a small sound. Quill did not look at him.

“I’m not supposed to say so. But it isn’t. The backup goes up clean, like he said. It reaches the gate. And it comes back with noise on it.” She touched the logs, and the flat line at the top of the climb opened out under her fingers into something finer, a fringe of grey along the gold. “Every one of the five did. We’re told to call it interference. It isn’t interference. Interference is random. This isn’t random.”
Noise. Sol heard Imogen Sallow’s low warm voice in the white corridor. A wrong note held under the music.
“What is it, then?”
“I don’t know.” Quill hesitated. “It has a shape. It repeats, but not exactly. If you put it through the speakers...” She glanced at the door, and then touched the log again.

The sound that came out of the rack was very faint. It was mostly hiss, the dry endless hiss of a line with nothing on it. But under the hiss there was something else, so low that Sol had to lean toward it: a rise and a fall, and a pause, and a rise and a fall again. It was not a voice. It was not music. It had the cadence, he thought, that the responses had in the cathedral at Abundance when you heard them from the vestry through a closed door, when you could not make out a single word and knew all the same that people were saying something together.
“Where does it come from?” he asked.
Quill looked up, not at him but at the low ceiling, as if she could see through the racks and the ice and the dark above Europa to wherever the line went.
“From inside,” she said. “From the City.”
The door opened. Fell came back in with the report in his hand, and Quill touched the log closed, and the hiss stopped.
“There you are, Your Grace,” Fell said cheerfully. “Hardware. I’ve put it all down.”

The chapel of the lower workings was hardly larger than a closet, with a single bench and a Pearl in the wall, but it was empty, and Sol asked Pell to wait outside. He knelt on the stone. He did not take the cushion.

He had been into the City of the Throne more times than he had stood before the Face. Every bishop had. One went in through the Pearl to comfort families, to carry messages, to look in on the newly ascended and bring back word that they were well. It was the plainest part of a bishop’s work. He touched his temple and asked, and the gold of the Pearl deepened and opened, and he went through.
His body stayed on its knees in the chapel. He knew that, as one knows in a dream that one is dreaming. But his sight went through the gold and came out the other side, and he stood in the City.

It was as it always was. The wall rose behind him, great and high, built of a stone like jasper, clear as crystal, and the gate he had come through was a single pearl. The street ran away before him and it was gold, pure gold, so fine and so clear that he could see through it, down and down, to more gold. There was no sun. There did not need to be. The light came from everywhere at once and nowhere, and it lay on the City the way the gold light had lain on the Bounty Market at noon. A river ran down the middle of the street, bright as glass. On either side of it grew trees heavy with fruit.

And the ascended were everywhere. They walked along the river in white, young and beautiful and unhurried. They sat at long tables in the open air that were piled with more food than the Bounty Market held on its best day, and they ate, and were served more, and ate. They passed through arcades where every stall held something lovelier than the last, and they took what they wanted, and wanted the next. They smiled. Every one of them smiled. Sol had walked here a thousand times, and he had always found it the most beautiful place he knew, and he found it beautiful now. He told himself that he did.

He had come, as always, for someone else’s dead. All down the long tables the places were laid and filled; somewhere along this street Nessa Amsel would have her Emmet beside her by now, in the seat she had saved him. No one here had laid a place for Sol. He had thought that once already, on the garden ring with cake on his fingers, and had not let himself mind it. He did not let himself mind it now.
“Joss Arden,” he said. “Drill crew, Serenity. Ascended today.”
The answer came the way answers came in the City, not as a voice but as a knowledge laid gently in his mind. There is no citizen of that name in the City of the Throne.
He had known it. He stood a moment in the light.
“Ada Arden,” he said. “Ascended from Serenity, the old south dome.”

She came almost at once. She came along the golden street from the direction of the river, a slender young woman in white with her son’s pale blue eyes, and she was smiling before she reached him, a wide warm smile of pure delight.
“Your Grace! What an honor. No one told me a bishop was coming.”
“I’ve come about your son.”
“Joss! He visits every week, you know. He’s such a good boy.” Her smile did not change. “Is he coming? He said he’d come.”
“There was an accident,” Sol said. “In the north shafts. He...” He stopped. There was no word in the liturgy for what he had to tell her. “He won’t be coming. Not today.”
“Oh, but he’ll come soon,” Ada Arden said. “Everyone comes. We’re so happy here, Your Grace. Tell him we’re so happy. Tell Rena too.”
Sol looked at her.

Her smile was perfect, and her voice was perfect, warm and bright and without a shadow in it. But her eyes were fixed on his, and they were very wide, and there was something in them that did not belong to the smile at all. He could not have said what it was. If he had seen it in a living face, in a face in the market or at the cathedral door, he would have said that she was asking him for something. That she was asking him for something with her whole strength, and could not say what, and was afraid he would not understand.
Then the City stuttered.

It lasted no longer than a heartbeat. The gold went flat and grey, as if the light had been taken out of everything at once, and the river stopped, and Ada Arden’s face hung before him with her mouth open on a word he could not hear, a word that was not happy, and her eyes still fixed on his.
Then the light was back. The river ran. She was smiling.
“We’re so happy here, Your Grace,” she said, in exactly the same voice, with exactly the same lift at the end. “Tell him we’re so happy.”
“Close,” Sol said.

He was on his knees on the stone of the chapel with the Pearl glowing gold and patient in front of him. His hands were cold. He did not know how long he had been kneeling. He did not know whether the pressure behind his eye had been there before he went through, or whether it had come with him back out.

Pell walked him back to their lodging through the Long Gallery under the lanterns. Jupiter had moved in its circles of glass. Pell talked a little about supper, and about the report, and asked whether he should tell the administrator in Concord that it was the relays after all, and Sol said, “Tell them nothing yet,” and Pell said, “Of course, Your Grace,” and did not ask anything more.

Sol did not sleep. He lay in the dark of the guest room with his eyes open and listened to the silence of Serenity. He thought about the gold line climbing and stopping. He thought about Rena Arden’s face coming apart and going smooth. He thought about a hiss with something under it, rising and falling, like people saying something together behind a closed door, and about a woman’s eyes in the City of the Throne. Every week. Same thing.

Some time before the middle of the night he gave up on sleep, and lit the lamp low, and sat at the little desk with the tablet Pell had left him and the failure files open on it: Vasque’s four from Abundance, and the five from Serenity. He had read them all before. He read them again, the way he would have read a text before preaching on it, and set beside each name what he had heard said of it.

The foreman who gave away his flowers. The courier on another woman’s run. The young man outside the gaming house, handing out his winnings, if the other man was to be believed. Ilse Dorn, sending back her stipend twice a year. Hanne Lusk, stepping out of the line at the chapel door. And now Joss Arden, sending half his pay to people he had never met, while his wife sat beside him and did not understand it.
He had not decided to write anything. But the stylus was in his hand, and in the margin under the names there was a word.
generous?

He looked at it for a long time. It made no sense. The City of the Throne was the reward of the kept; the Remembrance said so, and so had every day of his life. The wicked had been swept away. If the City ever refused anyone, it would refuse the cruel and the proud, the man who had wanted another man’s winnings and paid the family and gone back to the tables. Why would it refuse the kind?
He drew a line through the word. It stayed legible under the line, as crossed-out words do.

He went down through the files once more, past the cause and the priest and the times of submission, to the household fields at the bottom that no one ever read. Last Renewal. Household Pearl: in good order. Last Pearl visit.

The last was blank. He went back through the others. It was blank on all nine: not a date, not a name. In colonies where every household kept its anniversaries in the City, none of these nine had ever knelt at a Pearl to see anyone at all. Or no one had thought to write it down. A clerk’s omission, he told himself. Nine clerks’ omissions, on two worlds. But Joss Arden, who had given as freely as any of them, had knelt at a Pearl every week since he was a boy to see his mother. One such man was enough to make the rest careless clerks and not a pattern, and Sol let it go.

Somewhere in the last hour his left hand had gone into the drawer where Pell had laid out his stoles and come back with the little steel rule, and he found he was turning it over in his fingers, his thumb moving along the worn marks of the old measure, as it did whenever he was thinking. He put it back behind the stoles and shut the drawer.
He thought about the old man sitting on his bed with his back to the Pearl, looking at the ice because it was honest.
Come back when you’re tired of tidy answers.

A little after the middle of the night he put out the lamp and dressed in the dark, quietly, so as not to wake Pell in the next room. In the gallery the lanterns had dimmed to their night setting, and Jupiter was a faint banded ghost at the top of each shaft, and his weighted boots made no sound at all on the ice.
The night warden at the holding house was a young man with a gentle face who stood at once when he saw the robes.
“Your Grace. Is something wrong?”
“I want to see the prisoner Hale.”
The warden smiled, kindly, as if the bishop had made a small slip of the tongue that anyone might make at such an hour. “Our patient, Your Grace.”

Sol heard it then. Three days ago, on the floor of the Bounty Market, he had said it himself, in the voice he used in the cathedral, and a warden had bowed to it. He’s a patient, not a prisoner. He did not know when the other word had come into his mouth, or where it had come from.
“Our patient,” he said.
The warden led him down the white corridor, past the doors with their small dark panes, to the last room at the end. He touched the door, and it slid open without a sound on the blue dark inside.
